query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with densities below 6 g/cm3, controlled thermal aging promotes the segregation and precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds from an initially homogeneous solid-solution state. These precipitates act as nucleation sites for a continuous Mg–rich oxide scale during high-temperature exposure, thereby enhancing oxidation resistance, but the resulting microstructural heterogeneity also establishes localized galvanic couples that worsen corrosion behavior at room temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: A non-equilibrium, rapidly solidified or as-processed Mg-containing lightweight HEA with a largely homogeneous solid-solution structure and a fine distribution of constituent elements.
generation.intervention: Apply an aging or thermal exposure treatment designed to allow phase separation, whereby distinct Mg-rich intermetallic compounds begin to precipitate from the matrix.
generation.conditions: Test comparisons under high-temperature oxidation (e.g., in air at elevated temperatures relevant to service conditions) and room-temperature corrosion (e.g., exposure in an electrolyte solution) in controlled laboratory environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of microstructure via the segregation of Mg and formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates, which mediate both oxide-scale nucleation and local electrochemical heterogeneity.
generation.mechanism: Thermal aging of the non-equilibrium alloy induces the precipitation of Mg-rich phases that serve as preferential sites for the nucleation and coalescence of a continuous, protective Mg–rich oxide film under high-temperature conditions. In parallel, these phases generate electrochemical potential differences with the surrounding matrix, promoting localized galvanic corrosion during aqueous exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial homogeneous state, aged samples will exhibit improved high-temperature oxidation resistance (evidenced by more uniform, adherent oxide scales and possibly lower oxidation weight gain) but will show an accelerated corrosion rate at room temperature due to enhanced galvanic coupling between the intermetallic precipitates and the matrix.
generation.baseline: The as-processed alloy with a predominantly solid solution without significant phase segregation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to Mg-containing lightweight HEAs with a density below 6 g/cm3 and may be sensitive to the exact aging temperature, time, and alloy composition. Deviations in these parameters or in the processing route may influence the evolution pathway.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of the improvement in oxidation resistance versus the degradation in corrosion resistance and the precise role of different Mg-rich intermetallic species remains to be determined; differences in heat-treatment schedules might also affect phase evolution kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples with identical initial compositions and processing conditions. Subject one set to the thermal aging treatment (to induce Mg-rich intermetallic precipitation) and keep the other set as the as-processed baseline. Conduct systematic high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., isothermal air exposure at predetermined temperatures for fixed durations) and controlled corrosion testing (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization in a standard electrolyte). Use microstructural characterization (TEM, SEM, EDS) to correlate intermetallic phase distribution with oxidation scale characteristics and localized corrosion sites.
measurements: Oxidation weight gain and scale morphology
Phase identification and distribution via XRD and electron microscopy
Electrochemical corrosion parameters (corrosion potential, current density)
Surface potential mapping to assess galvanic effects
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in the uniformity or adherence of the high-temperature oxide scale compared to the baseline, or if the corrosion rate does not increase due to localized galvanic coupling (or even decreases) relative to the as-processed state, then the hypothesis that phase segregation mediates the dual effects on oxidation and corrosion would be falsified.
